The correct answer is B.

In this question, the easiest way to identify the correct rotation is to look at the edges and surfaces that meet at each marked vertex. The position of the dot on the screen may change completely after rotation, but the parts of the object surrounding that vertex must remain the same.

Start with the curved shape. Follow the marked corner and notice how it sits next to the curved edge and the smaller side surface. Several options place the dot on a different end of the shape, so they can be eliminated.

Now check the long, pointed shape. In the model, the dot is attached to a specific corner next to the narrow face. Only in option B does this relationship remain unchanged after the object is rotated.

Therefore, B is the correct answer.

Then look at the E. The marked point must remain attached to the same part of the letter relative to its horizontal and vertical strokes.

Only option C shows both letters correctly rotated while keeping both dots in their original positions.

Therefore, C is the correct answer.

Solving Tip: With familiar shapes such as letters, use their distinctive parts as landmarks.

questions.question: The two objects in the top box are shown again in five options, rotated. Which option shows the same two objects, with the dot on the corresponding corner of each object?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A.

Start with the object on the left. The dot is located on the upper sloping section of the shape. Follow that section as the object is turned rather than focusing on whether the dot appears at the top, bottom, left, or right.

In option A, the marked vertex remains connected to the same surrounding edges.

Now check the second object. Its dot is beside one of the distinctive inward sections of the shape. Option A preserves this marked position as well.

The other options move at least one dot to a different vertex.

Therefore, A is the correct answer.

Solving Tip: A rotation can completely change the object's orientation on the page, but it cannot change which edges meet at the marked vertex.

A: trapezoid standing on end, dot at the top corner of its top edge — the same upper-sloping-section vertex; X-block turned, dot at the tip of its upper-right arm — the same arm tip after rotation. Both dots remain connected to the same edges — correct.
B: trapezoid standing, dot at its top-left corner; X-block turned, dot in the inner notch between two arms. Both dots moved to different vertices — mismatch.
C: trapezoid lying flat, dot at the bottom-left corner of its lower edge; X-block turned, dot at the bottom tip of a lower arm. Both dots moved — mismatch.

D: trapezoid near model orientation, dot on the top edge partway along the upper sloping section; X-block seen from the side, dot inside a notch on its right. At least one dot is on a different vertex — mismatch.
E: trapezoid standing tall, dot partway down its right edge; X-block turned, dot at the top of an upper arm but on the wrong arm. Mismatch.

questions.question: The two objects in the top box are shown again in five options, rotated. Which option shows the same two objects, with the dot on the corresponding corner of each object?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A.

The important feature to notice in this question is that the two dots are placed on different kinds of corner. On the plate the dot is on an outer corner of the near face, the one furthest from the notch. On the chevron it is on the inner corner of the notch, where the shape folds back into itself. A rotation can never turn an inner corner into an outer one.

Let's begin with the chevron, since that distinction is quick to check. Any option that moves its dot onto an outer corner is eliminated at once, without your having to look at its plate at all.

The plate then separates the remaining options, and here the face decides rather than the corner. The plate is a slab, so every corner of its outline exists twice, once on each broad face. Options that show the plate from its other side present the mirror partner of the marked corner, not the marked corner itself.

*Notice! One of the wrong options looks almost identical to the model. When that happens, check which face of the slab you are being shown before you accept it.

scene.note: Object 1 (left): a thick square plate with a diagonal notch cut out of its lower-right side — dot on the top-left outer corner of the near face, the corner furthest from the notch. Object 2 (right): a thick chevron (bent arrow plate) — dot on the inner corner of its notch, where the shape folds back into itself.

A: plate with its notch at the lower left, dot at the top corner of its right edge — the same near-face outer corner after rotation; chevron lying like a roof, dot at the inner end of its right arm, still an inner notch corner. Both dots correspond — correct.

B: plate with its notch opening upward, dot at the bottom-left corner; chevron near-upright, dot at the bottom tip of its lower arm — an outer corner. The chevron dot has moved from inner to outer — mismatch.

C: plate dot at its top-right corner; chevron tipped over, dot at its inner notch corner. The plate is shown from its other side, so its dot is the mirror partner corner, not the marked one — mismatch.

D: plate dot at its top-left corner, looking almost identical to the model — but the plate is shown from its other face, so this is the mirror partner of the marked corner (the trap named in the explanation); chevron lying flat, dot on the inner edge of its right arm. Mismatch.

questions.question: Two separate objects are placed at the center of the screen, each with a dot placed in one corner. The answer choices contain the same two objects, rotated in some way. Choose the option that shows both the dots placed in the same corners as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is B.

Neither object here is symmetrical, so every vertex has a unique position and no two corners are comparable. That makes the anchor sentence reliable once you write it.

The bracket's marked vertex is on the inside of the elbow, where the diagonal arm meets the upright. The plate's marked vertex is where its top edge meets its one slanted edge.

Let's begin with the plate, which is the faster of the two to rotate mentally. Because it has exactly one slanted edge, naming the pair of edges that meet at the dot pins the corner down completely, and that pairing survives any rotation. Options that place the dot at a corner between two straight sides are eliminated.

Bring in the bracket only for the options that survive. Watch the elbow: a dot on the outside of the elbow looks much like a dot on the inside once the object has been turned, but they are different corners.

scene.note: Object 1 (left): an elbow bracket — an upright post with a diagonal arm angling down to the right — dot on the inside of the elbow, at the underside tip where the diagonal arm meets the upright. Object 2 (right): a thick quadrilateral plate with one slanted edge (its left side) — dot at the top corner where the top edge meets the slanted edge.
A: bracket lying as an L, dot at the tip of its horizontal foot — the outside end, not the inside of the elbow; plate upright, dot at the top of its left edge. The bracket dot is wrong — mismatch.

B: bracket lying on its back as a step shape, dot at the top of the diagonal step — the inside-of-elbow vertex carried round; plate tilted, dot at its bottom point — the corner where the top edge and the slanted edge meet, after rotation. Both dots correspond — correct.
C: bracket tipped, dot at the left tip of its angled foot; plate near-upright, dot at its top-right corner — a corner between two straight sides, which the explanation eliminates. Mismatch.
D: bracket lying as an L, dot at the top of its upright step; plate standing, dot at its bottom-left corner — again a straight-sided corner. Mismatch.

E: bracket in almost the model orientation, dot at the arm's underside tip; plate tilted, dot on its slanted edge partway down rather than at the corner where the slant meets the top edge. The plate dot is not at the vertex — mismatch.

questions.question: The two objects in the top box are shown again in five options, rotated. Which option shows the same two objects, with the dot on the corresponding corner of each object?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is C.

Notice that the rounded object is much easier to work with. A curve has no corners, so this shape offers only three possible positions for a dot: the tip where the two straight edges meet, and the two junctions where those straight edges run into the curve. The two junctions are distinguishable because the straight edges are of different lengths.

Let's begin there. The marked vertex in the model is the junction at the end of the longer straight edge. Options that place the dot at the other junction, or along the curve itself where no corner exists, are eliminated immediately.

Only then is the trapezoid needed, read by the corner where its longest and shortest edges meet.

*Notice! Whenever one of the two objects has a curve, start with it. A curve is poor at hiding a corner, which is exactly what you want under time pressure.

Object 2 (right): a tall trapezoid prism with a long slanted left edge and a small step near its bottom — dot on the slanted edge at the small step, the corner where its longest and shortest edges meet.

B: rounded plate turned over, dot at the right-hand junction — the junction at the end of the shorter straight edge, not the longer one; trapezoid tilted, dot on its slanted edge at the step. The rounded object's dot is at the wrong junction — mismatch.

C: rounded plate turned over, dot at the junction at the right — the end of the longer straight edge after the turn; trapezoid upside down, dot at the top of its slanted edge — the corner where the longest and shortest edges meet. Both dots correspond — correct.
D: rounded plate near-upright, dot on its right straight edge partway down — not at a junction; trapezoid upside down, dot on its left edge near the top. Both dots off the vertices — mismatch.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is D.

The most important feature to notice in this question is that the squared C on the left is symmetrical: turned over, it lands back on itself. Its upper and lower arms are therefore comparable positions, and a dot on the inner corner of one is comparable to a dot on the inner corner of the other. This object cannot decide the question by itself.

Let's begin with the wavy ribbon instead. Its top edge dips and rises, so its two upper ends are genuinely different — one sits where the wave begins to fall, the other where it comes back up — and the marked vertex is the higher of them. The bottom edge of the sheet is straight, so any option placing the dot there is eliminated at once.

Once the ribbon has narrowed the field, the bracket only has to be consistent with what remains.

*Notice! Do not try to eliminate on the square bracket. On a symmetrical object, two corners that look different can be the same corner.

scene.note: Object 1 (left): a squared letter-C bracket (thick C profile, symmetrical top-to-bottom) — dot on the inner corner of its lower arm. Object 2 (right): a wavy ribbon — a thin sheet whose top edge dips and rises in a wave while its bottom edge is straight — dot at the top of the right-hand peak, the higher of its two upper ends.

E: C-bracket mirrored, dot on the inner corner of its lower arm (consistent, but the C cannot decide the question); ribbon upside down, dot at its bottom-right corner — on the straight bottom edge. Eliminated on the ribbon — mismatch.

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is B.

These shapes look like pictures, but they should be treated as geometry.

Notice that the crescent is much easier to rotate mentally: it has only two horns, so the dot is on one of them and you need only decide which horn and which face. The marked vertex in the model is the horn at the outer end of the longer curve.

Let's begin there. Options that move the dot to the other horn, or place it partway along the curve rather than at a horn, are eliminated.

*Notice! A crescent that has been turned over still curves much the same way at a glance, but its two horns have swapped. Check which side the band of thickness is on.

scene.note: Object 1 (left): a sun — a flat disc ringed with irregular blocky spikes — dot on the left-hand spike, at the point where that spike meets the disc. Object 2 (right): a thick crescent plate — dot at the upper horn tip, the horn at the outer end of the longer curve.
A: sun near-upright, dot on an upper-left spike; crescent upright, dot at its lower horn tip — the other horn, so A is eliminated on the crescent. Mismatch.

B: sun turned, dot at the base of a bottom spike — the same spike counted round from the spike that sits differently against the disc; crescent lying with its horns up, dot at the right horn tip — the horn at the outer end of the longer curve, on the correct face. Both dots correspond — correct.

D: sun tipped, dot on an upper-left spike; crescent as an arch, dot on the right side of the arch — partway along the curve, not at a horn. Eliminated on the crescent — mismatch.

E: sun near-upright, dot on the left spike as in the model; crescent tipped, dot at its right (lower) horn tip — the horns have swapped because the crescent has been turned over. The crescent dot is on the wrong horn — mismatch.

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is D.

Notice that it is much easier to mentally rotate the right object, so the elimination should begin there.

The bar has one square-cut end and one rounded end, and its marked vertex is a corner of the square end. Because the bar carries so few features, its face matters as much as its corner: the same end seen from the other side is not the same corner, and the wrong options rely on that.

*Notice! When one of the two objects is much simpler than the other, the simple one is not the one to skip. It is the one to work with.

scene.note: Object 1 (left): a jagged star plate (flat, four uneven points) — dot at the inner corner at the base of its long right-pointing spike, near the centre of the star. Object 2 (right): a long bar with one square-cut end and one rounded end — dot at a corner of the square-cut end (its top corner as drawn).

A: star standing vertical, dot at its centre inner corner; bar tilted, dot at its lower end corner — the same end seen from the other side is not the same corner (per the explanation), so the bar fails. Mismatch.
B: star near model orientation, dot at an inner corner on its right; bar point-down, dot at its bottom tip. The bar's dot is not on the square-end corner on the correct face — mismatch.

The dart is folded along a crease, and that crease divides it into two faces, so every corner belongs to one side of the fold or the other. That is the description to use when you reach it.

Let's begin with the wedge, which is the simpler object. Its marked vertex is unusual and therefore useful: the dot is placed partway along a long edge rather than at an extreme point of the shape. Options that move it to a true corner of the wedge are eliminated.

scene.note: Object 1 (left): a dart — a thin sheet folded along a centre crease into two triangular faces — dot at the top apex tip of the dart, on one side of the fold. Object 2 (right): an elongated wedge prism — dot partway along one of its long edges, not at a corner.
A: dart upside down, dot at its bottom tip; wedge lying flat as a slab, dot on its top edge near a corner — a true corner, which the explanation eliminates. Mismatch.

B: dart near-upright, dot at its top tip on the crease side; wedge tipped, dot at a corner of its small end — again a true corner rather than partway along the long edge. Eliminated on the wedge — mismatch.

C: dart lying on its side, dot at its left tip — the apex corner on the same side of the fold; wedge standing vertical, dot on its front face partway along the long edge. Both dots correspond — correct.
D: dart folded the other way, dot at the inner crease point at its centre; wedge lying flat, dot at a corner of its end face. Both dots wrong — mismatch.

E: dart lying flat, dot at its top tip; wedge standing, dot on its right edge partway along — but on the wrong long edge/face relative to the fold side of the dart pairing. At least one dot does not correspond — mismatch.

questions.question: Two separate objects are placed at the center of the screen, each with a dot placed in one corner. The answer choices contain the same two objects, rotated in some way. Choose the option that shows both the dots placed in the same corners as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is E.

In this question you are asked to rotate two letters, and letters can be read, which makes the first step much faster than it looks. For each option, ask whether the letters have been turned within their own plane or turned over. A letter turned over reads as its mirror image, and an M turned upside down reads as a W.

Then check the dots against the model. On the P, the dot is inside the bowl, at the lower-left corner of the inner opening, on the face towards you. On the M, it is at the inner corner where the second diagonal meets the right-hand stem, also on the near face.

Both conditions have to hold at once: the two letters turned consistently, and both dots still on the corners described above.

*Notice! Turning a letter over swaps its front and back, so a dot inside the bowl of the P can end up appearing outside it. In this question the face is what decides.

scene.note: Object 1 (left): an extruded letter P — dot inside the bowl, at the lower-left corner of the inner opening, on the near face. Object 2 (right): an extruded letter M — dot at the inner corner where the second diagonal meets the right-hand stem, on the near face.

A: P turned over (reads as a mirrored shape) with no dot visible inside its bowl — the dot has ended up on the far face; M upside down reading as a W, dot at the bottom of its first valley. The P's face is wrong — mismatch.

B: P turned in its plane (reads like a 9), dot inside its bowl at the lower part; M on its side like a Σ, dot at the end of its top arm — not the inner corner where the diagonal meets the stem. The M dot is wrong — mismatch.
C: P on its side with no dot visible in the bowl; M upside down as a W, dot at the bottom of its first valley — an outer valley corner, not the diagonal-to-stem inner corner. Mismatch.
D: P tilted diagonally, dot on the edge of its bowl; M on its side like a Σ, dot at the end of its bottom arm. Both dots on different corners — mismatch.

E: P lying on its side with the bowl opening downward, dot still inside the bowl at the corresponding inner corner on the near face; M/W tilted, dot at the inner corner where a diagonal meets its stem. Both letters turned consistently and both dots on the described corners — correct.

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is D.

Notice that the figure '8' is symmetrical when horizontal, but not when vertical (the two holes vary in size); therefore, option D is correct (comparable corner is marked in red) and option B is not (the correct corner is marked in green).

scene.note: Object 1 (left): an extruded digit 1 (with a base serif) — dot at the bottom of the base, on the front face at the left end of the base bar. Object 2 (right): an extruded digit 8 (upper hole smaller than the lower hole) — dot at the middle pinch on the right side, where the two loops meet.
A: 1 upright, dot at the bottom-left of its base as in the model; 8 lying horizontal (like ∞), dot inside its left loop. The 8's dot is not on the comparable pinch corner — mismatch.

B: 1 lying horizontal, dot at the tip of its right end; 8 upright, dot at the middle pinch on the left side. Per the explanation, B is not correct: with the 8 vertical its two holes differ in size, so the left-side pinch is not the comparable corner (the correct corner is marked in green in the source's diagram). Mismatch.
C: 1 upside down, dot on its top bar; 8 upright, dot at the middle pinch on the right side as in the model. The 1's dot is on the wrong part — mismatch.

D: 1 lying horizontal with its dot on the corresponding base corner (partly hidden on the underside as drawn); 8 lying horizontal (like ∞), dot inside the right loop at the comparable pinch corner (marked in red in the source's diagram). With the 8 horizontal it is symmetrical, so this corner is comparable — correct.
E: 1 tilted into a Z-like orientation, dot at its top corner; 8 lying flat with no dot clearly visible on the pinch. The 1's dot is wrong — mismatch.

questions.question: The two objects in the top box are shown again in five options, rotated. Which option shows the same two objects, with the dot on the corresponding corner of each object?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is E.

Since the cross-like object has several different angles (unlike the triangle, the cross is not symmetrical), it is important to make sure that the dot is placed at the correct point, even before starting the rotation.

scene.note: Object 1 (left): a thin right-triangle plate — dot at the apex at the top of the tall edge, where the long slanted edge begins. Object 2 (right): an irregular cross block (plus-shaped, arms of different lengths, not symmetrical) — dot at the inner corner on the front face where the left arm meets the vertical arm, just left of centre.
A: triangle upright, dot at the bottom-left corner (bottom of the tall edge) instead of the apex; cross turned, dot at its centre on the horizontal arm. Both dots on different points — mismatch.
B: triangle tilted, dot on its slanted edge near the apex point; cross lying on its side, dot at the centre on an arm's inner corner — a different angle of the cross. Mismatch.

C: triangle tilted, dot at its apex as in the model; cross upside down, dot at the centre on its vertical arm below the crossbar — a different inner corner of the non-symmetrical cross. The cross dot is wrong — mismatch.
D: triangle upright, dot at its bottom-left corner; cross near-upright, dot near the top of the junction between its arms. Both dots on different points — mismatch.

E: triangle lying with its tall edge horizontal, dot at the bottom-right corner — the apex carried round by the rotation; cross lying on its side, dot at the inner corner where the (now upper) arm meets the crossbar, the same point as the model. Both dots correspond — correct.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is C.

The most important feature to notice in this question is that the block on the right is close to symmetrical: it is a bar with tabs on opposite sides, so several of its corners are comparable positions. That object cannot decide the question by itself.

Let's begin with the bent plate on the left. It is folded twice, and those folds divide it into panels of different sizes, so every corner belongs to a nameable panel and a nameable edge. In the model the dot is on an outer corner of the widest panel, on the near face. Options that place it on one of the narrow panels are eliminated at once.

Only then bring in the block, and use it to confirm rather than to choose.

*Notice! When one of the two objects has repeating tabs or arms, do not start there. On a symmetrical object two corners that look different can be the same corner.

scene.note: Left object: a bent plate folded twice into three panels of different sizes (widest panel at the bottom as drawn). Its dot is on an outer corner of the widest panel, on the near face (bottom-left tip of the widest panel as drawn). Right object: a near-symmetrical block — a bar with tabs on opposite sides. Its dot is on the bottom-front corner of the main bar, near face (lower-left corner as drawn).
Option A: pair lying flatter. Bent-plate dot sits on a corner of one of the narrow panels (top end as drawn), not the widest panel — mismatch. Block dot on a lower corner of the right-hand tab.

Option B: bent plate tipped up with its dot at the bottom tip; the tabbed block is shown smaller/turned with its dot on a lower corner of a tab. The plate dot is not on the outer corner of the widest panel on the near face in the model's sense — eliminated on the plate/block check.

Option C (correct): bent plate rotated so the widest panel is uppermost-left; its dot is on the outer corner of the widest panel, near face (left tip as drawn). Block turned to a cross-like view; its dot is on the corresponding tab corner (upper-right as drawn). Both dots correspond to the model.

Option D: bent-plate dot at the left end of the widest panel, but the block is shown face-on as a plus/cross with its dot on the left protruding tab — not the corresponding corner of the bar, so the pair fails on the block.
Option E: bent plate lying almost flat, no dot visible on it (dot on the hidden/underside face) — cannot be the near-face widest-panel corner. Block dot on a lower corner of the right tab.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is B.

In this question the left object carries a single sharp spike, and that spike is the most valuable landmark on either shape. Everything else on the plate is a fold or a flat panel, but there is only one spike, so any corner can be described by its position relative to it.

Let's begin there. In the model the dot sits in the concave corner at the base of the spike, on the near face — not on the spike's tip and not on an outer edge. Any option that moves the dot onto an outer corner is eliminated, because no rotation converts a concave corner into a convex one.

The faceted block on the right is the slower read and should be used only on the options that survive.

scene.note: Left object: a flat folded plate carrying a single sharp spike. Its dot sits in the concave corner at the base of the spike, on the near face — not on the spike's tip and not on an outer edge. Right object: an irregular faceted block. Its dot is on a lower corner of one facet on the near face (right-hand edge as drawn).

Option A: spiked plate tipped up; its dot is on an outer (convex) corner near the spike, not the concave corner at the spike's base — mismatch. Faceted block shown as a plain drum-like form with dot at the bottom.

Option B (correct): spiked plate rotated so the spike points down-left; its dot remains in the concave corner at the base of the spike, near face. Faceted block rotated with its dot on the corresponding facet corner (top as drawn). Both dots correspond.

Option C: spiked-plate dot moved onto an outer corner at the tail end of the plate — a rotation cannot turn the concave spike-base corner into this convex corner. Faceted block dot at its bottom-right tip.
Option D: spiked plate folded view with dot on a bottom outer corner — mismatch on the plate. Faceted block dot on its right-hand edge corner.

Option E: spiked plate close to the model orientation with dot near the spike's base notch, but the right-hand block is shown as a plain box-like form with its dot on the top face — the faceted block's dot is on the wrong facet, so the pair fails on the block.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A.

Letters can be read, which makes the first step much faster than it looks. For each option, ask whether the letters have been turned within their own plane or turned over. A letter turned over reads as its mirror image, and a T turned upside down reads as ⊥.

Then check the dots. On the T the dot is at the left end of the crossbar, on the near face. On the E it is at the outer end of the bottom arm.

*Notice! The E is the object to be careful with. Its top and bottom arms are similar in length, so "the end of an outer arm" describes two corners, not one. You must say which arm and which face, or you will find two options that both seem to fit.

scene.note: Left object: a block letter T. Its dot is at the left end of the crossbar, on the near face. Right object: a block letter E (tilted as drawn). Its dot is at the outer end of the bottom arm, on the near face.

Option A (correct): T turned upside down within its own plane (reads as an inverted T); its dot stays at the end of the crossbar on the near face (now at the bottom as drawn). E upright, not mirrored; its dot is at the outer end of the bottom arm. Both correspond.
Option B: T lying on its side with dot at an end of the stem; the E is turned over so it reads as its mirror image — a rotation in the plane cannot produce it. Mismatch.
Option C: letters in near-model orientation, but the E's dot sits at the end of the middle arm rather than the outer end of the bottom arm — wrong arm. Mismatch.
Option D: both letters tipped diagonally; the E lies on its back with its dot at the top corner of an outer arm on the far face — not the bottom arm's outer end on the near face. Mismatch.
Option E: T on its side pointing left with dot at the stem end; E upright but its dot is on the far face at the bottom arm's end — face is wrong. Mismatch.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is D.

When flipping both K and H vertically, the dot on K is situated on the bottom-rear side of it, and the dot on H is situated on the front end of its upper-horizontal line, just as in the model.

Answer option E is incorrect: when turning both letters from left to right on the horizontal axis, the dot on K appears to be the same as in the model, but the dot on H appears on the rear end of its bottom-horizontal line.

*Notice! The H is symmetrical in outline, so the letter itself cannot tell you whether you are looking at its front or its rear. Only the dot can. This is why the K, which is not symmetrical, should be read first.

scene.note: Left object: a block letter K. Its dot is on the bottom-rear side of the K, at the foot of the lower diagonal leg (bottom tip as drawn). Right object: a block letter H. Its dot is on the front end of its upper-horizontal line (on the right upright at crossbar height, near face, as drawn).
Option A: both letters tipped/lying over; the H lies on its side and its dot is not on the front end of the upper-horizontal line. Mismatch.

Option B: K tilted with its dot at the junction of the diagonals (mid-letter) rather than the bottom-rear foot; H upright with its dot on the left upright — wrong end of the horizontal line. Mismatch.
Option C: both letters lying flat (seen from above at an angle); dots sit on top faces/edges that do not correspond to the model's bottom-rear K corner and front upper-horizontal H corner. Mismatch.

Option D (correct): both letters flipped vertically. The K's dot stays on its bottom-rear side (carried to the top by the flip, rear face), and the H's dot stays on the front end of its upper-horizontal line, just as in the model. Both correspond.

Option E: both letters turned left-to-right on the horizontal axis. The K's dot appears the same as in the model, but the H's dot appears on the rear end of its bottom-horizontal line — wrong line and wrong end. Mismatch (per the explanation).

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is D.

The frame on the left is a closed triangular ring, so it has three outer corners and three inner ones, and the dot in the model sits on an inner corner — inside the opening, at the end of the narrowest side. Inner and outer corners can never be exchanged by a rotation, which removes several options immediately.

The arrow is the object to run first, though. It has a head with two barbs and a tapering tail, so its corners differ sharply from one another, and the dot in the model is at the tip of one barb. Options that move it to the tail, or to the other barb, are eliminated.

Bring in the frame only to separate what survives, and read the inner corner rather than the outline.

scene.note: Left object: a closed triangular frame (ring) with three outer corners and three inner corners. Its dot sits on an inner corner — inside the opening, at the end of the narrowest side (lower-right inner corner as drawn). Right object: an arrow with a head of two barbs and a tapering tail. Its dot is at the tip of one barb of the head (upper barb as drawn).
Option A: frame dot on an inner corner, but the arrow's dot is at the tail end, not a barb tip — mismatch on the arrow.
Option B: frame dot on an inner corner; arrow inverted with its dot on a corner of the head beside the barb rather than at the barb's tip — mismatch on the arrow.
Option C: arrow dot at a barb tip, but the frame's dot sits on the inner corner at the end of a different (wider) side, not the end of the narrowest side — mismatch on the frame.
Option D (correct): frame dot on the inner corner at the end of the narrowest side, inside the opening; arrow rotated with its dot at the tip of the same barb (lower tip as drawn). Both correspond.
Option E: frame stretched diagonally with dot at a bottom corner of the opening; the second object is shown folded with its dot on an upper corner of the head block, not at a barb tip — mismatch.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is E.

Both objects here are angular, but they are not equally useful. The block is the simpler of the two and should carry the elimination: it has one clear notch cut into it, and the dot in the model sits on a corner of that notch, on the near face. Options that move the dot to a corner of the plain outline are eliminated.

The spiked plate has many similar-looking points, which makes it expensive to read and easy to misjudge. If you need it, do not say "that spike" — count round from the spike that differs from the rest.

*Notice! On a shape with repeated points, a dot's position must be counted, not pointed at. This is the family where people lose the most time.

scene.note: Left object: a simple angular block with one clear notch cut into it. Its dot sits on a corner of that notch, on the near face (top corner as drawn). Right object: a spiked plate with many similar-looking points. Its dot is on a corner part-way round the outline (left-hand edge as drawn), counted from the spike that differs from the rest.
Option A: block dot moved to a corner of the plain outline (right tip as drawn), not a notch corner — mismatch on the block. Spiked plate rotated with dot near a lower point.
Option B: block tipped with dot at its bottom tip (plain outline corner); spiked plate dot at a bottom corner — mismatch on the block.
Option C: block dot on a lower outline corner; spiked plate (shown as a plain slab) dot on its left edge — the block's dot is not on the notch corner. Mismatch.
Option D: block dot at its bottom tip (plain outline); spiked plate dot at its right-hand tip — counted position does not match the model. Mismatch.

Option E (correct): block shown near-upright with its dot on the notch corner (bottom corner as drawn after rotation), near face; spiked plate stood on end with its dot at the counted corresponding point (bottom tip as drawn). Both correspond.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A.

Notice that the rounded object is far easier to work with than it first appears. Its surface is smooth, so it offers almost no corners — but it has one small notch along its edge, and that notch is the only nameable feature on the whole shape. The dot in the model sits right beside it.

Let's begin there. Any option that places the dot away from the notch is eliminated without further thought, and this single check clears most of the field. Then decide the face: because the pouch is a shell, the same point on its rim can be shown from either side.

The angular plate is the slower object and should confirm the survivor.

*Notice! A smooth object is not a hard object. The fewer features it has, the more decisive the ones it does have.

scene.note: Left object: an angular plate (blocky, stepped outline). Its dot is on its top corner (apex as drawn). Right object: a smooth rounded pouch/shell with almost no corners and one small notch along its edge. Its dot sits right beside that notch (right-hand edge as drawn). The pouch is modeled as a flattened sphere; its shape detail is in this note.

Option A (correct): angular plate lying on its side with dot on the corresponding corner (right side as drawn); pouch tipped up with its dot right beside the small notch (upper-right edge as drawn). Both correspond.
Option B: pouch shown long and low with its dot at the bottom tip, away from the notch — mismatch on the pouch. Plate dot on a right-hand corner.
Option C: pouch shown from the other side with its dot at the top corner, away from the notch — mismatch on the pouch. Plate dot on its right edge.
Option D: pouch lying flat with its dot at the right-hand tip, away from the notch — mismatch on the pouch. Plate dot at its top corner.

Option E: plate inverted with dot at its bottom tip; pouch shown open-side up with dot on its left rim — the dot is not beside the notch in the model's sense and the plate corner does not correspond. Mismatch.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is D.

The most important feature to notice is that the clover has four similar lobes arranged around a centre. Turned by a quarter, it lands back on itself, so its lobes are comparable positions and it cannot settle the question.

Let's begin with the C-ring instead. A ring with a gap has exactly two ends, and they are genuinely different, so the dot is at one of them and you need only decide which end and which face. Options that move the dot onto the body of the ring, away from either end, are eliminated at once.

Once the ring has narrowed the field, the clover only has to be consistent.

*Notice! Do not try to eliminate on the clover. This is the clearest example in the set of an object whose symmetry makes its corners interchangeable.

scene.note: Left object: a clover — four similar lobes arranged around a centre (modeled as a flattened sphere; lobe detail in this note). Its dot is at the centre where the lobes meet. Because of the four-fold symmetry the clover cannot settle the question. Right object: a C-ring — a ring with a gap, giving exactly two genuinely different ends (modeled as a part-turned cylinder). Its dot is at one end of the ring (the lower end of the gap as drawn).
Option A: clover dot at centre (consistent, but the clover cannot decide). C-ring dot at an end seen from the inner side — wrong end/face combination for the model's dot. Mismatch on the ring.
Option B: clover dot at centre. C-ring viewed from behind with its dot at the bottom end — the dot is on the same end but the wrong face of the ring. Mismatch on the ring.
Option C: clover shown without a visible centre dot (dot on the far side); C-ring dot at the left tip on the body end — not the model's end/face. Mismatch.
Option D (correct): clover dot at centre, consistent with the model. C-ring rotated with its dot at the same end of the gap and on the same face as in the model (lower end as drawn). Both correspond.
Option E: clover dot at centre. C-ring dot at the top end of the gap — the other end from the model's dot. Mismatch on the ring.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is C.

When turning the image on the left to the right, positioning it as it appears in the model, the dot on it appears to be located similarly to the location of the dot in the model. When positioning the image on the right the same way as in the model, the dot on it also appears in the same location as in the model.

*Notice! The figures in this question are drawn small, which tempts candidates to judge by overall shape. Overall shape is exactly what a rotation changes. Work corner by corner, and take the two objects one at a time rather than comparing the pair at a glance.

scene.note: Figures drawn small in the original. Left object: a double-arrow plate — a vertical shaft with an arrowhead at the top pointing up and a second arrowhead halfway down pointing right. Its dot is in the concave corner at the base of the right-pointing arrowhead, on the near face. Right object: an L-shaped bent arrow — a horizontal bar turning up at the right into an arrowhead. Its dot is at the inner corner at the base of the arrowhead (top of the riser), on the near face.

Option A: double-arrow plate tipped over with dot near the right-pointing head's tip area; bent arrow inverted with its dot at the lower tip — neither dot is in the model's concave base corner. Mismatch.
Option B: double-arrow plate upright with dot at the mid-shaft junction (not the arrowhead-base notch); bent arrow pointing down with dot at the arrowhead's bottom tip. Mismatch.

Option C (correct): double-arrow plate rotated diagonally with its dot in the concave corner at the base of the right-pointing arrowhead; bent arrow rotated with its dot at the inner corner at the base of its arrowhead. Both dots in the same corners as in the model.
Option D: double-arrow plate with dot at a top outer corner of the shaft; bent arrow with dot at a lower inner corner of the bend — not the arrowhead base. Mismatch.

Option E: double-arrow plate lying diagonally with dot in an upper notch; the second object shown as a plain bar with its dot on the top edge — the bent-arrow's arrowhead-base corner is absent. Mismatch.

questions.question: Below are two separate objects, each has a dot placed in one corner, and each has five possible rotations. Choose the answer option in which the dots are placed in the same corners of the objects as in the model.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A.

The box on the right is the object to start with. It is a plain rectangular block except for one detail: a diagonal crease across one of its faces. That crease turns an otherwise featureless box into a readable object, because it identifies which face you are looking at and which corner of that face the dot belongs to. In the model the dot sits at the corner where the crease meets the edge.

Options that place the dot at a corner away from the crease, or on a face that carries no crease at all, are eliminated.

The pinwheel on the left has curved blades that repeat around a centre, so it is the harder of the two and should be left to confirm the answer.

*Notice! When a simple object carries one distinguishing mark, that mark is worth more than all the detail on the complicated object beside it.

scene.note: Left object: a pinwheel — curved blades repeating around a centre (modeled as a flat cylinder; blade detail in this note). Its dot sits on one blade near the centre hub (small and hard to read at capture size — see note file flag). Right object: a plain rectangular block with one detail — a diagonal crease across one face. Its dot sits at the corner where the crease meets the edge (lower-right corner of the creased face as drawn).
Option A (correct): block tilted with its dot at the corner where the diagonal crease meets the edge; pinwheel consistent with the model. Both correspond.
Option B: pinwheel dot visible on its rim at the left; block dot on a left-hand corner of a face — away from the corner where the crease meets the edge. Mismatch on the block.
Option C: block dot on the right edge of a face that carries no crease — eliminated per the explanation. Pinwheel shown from the other side, no dot visible.
Option D: pinwheel seen edge-on inside a drum-like view; block dot at a lower-left corner of a plain face, away from the crease — mismatch on the block.
Option E: pinwheel with a star-like centre; block dot in the middle of the creased face where the crease crosses, not at the corner where the crease meets the edge — mismatch on the block.

questions.question: The following cube has six different facets. Which of the four possible options represents the same cube shown from a different perspective?
questions.explanation:
We were told the cube has six different facets. Therefore, each facet is unique- even the white one. Therefore, when you see a white facet in the answers, you should regard it as representing the one shown in the question.
• The first option on the left can be eliminated because the facet facing the front should be white.
• The second option is correct and reveals the bottom facet of the cube that was hidden in the main diagram.
• The third option can be eliminated because the white facet should be at the back of the cube rather than in front.
• The fourth option on the right can be eliminated because the white facet should be on the left side rather than on the right.
